corrected_draft.title: Trump Grants Steve Bannon Clemency in Final Hours
corrected_draft.description_short: Trump granted Steve Bannon clemency on Jan. 19, 2021, while Bannon faced We Build the Wall-related federal charges and had pleaded not guilty.
corrected_draft.description_medium: Reuters reported that Donald Trump granted clemency to Steve Bannon during a wave of pardons and commutations in his final hours on January 19, 2021. Bannon had been charged with defrauding supporters who donated to the We Build the Wall effort and had pleaded not guilty. DOJ’s clemency list identifies conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The claim about whether Bannon filed a clemency petition is not established here.
corrected_draft.description_long: On January 19, 2021, in the final hours of his presidency, Donald Trump granted clemency to former White House aide Steve Bannon as part of a larger group of pardons and commutations. Reuters reported the grant on January 20 and described Bannon as having been charged the prior year with defrauding supporters who contributed to a private effort to build a border wall; he had pleaded not guilty. The Justice Department’s clemency list names Bannon and identifies conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. These sources support a discrete clemency action before the federal case reached trial. They do not establish whether Bannon submitted a petition through the Office of the Pardon Attorney, so the record should not assert that no petition was filed. It should also attribute the fraud allegations to the pending charges and avoid treating them as a conviction.

corrected_draft.title: DOJ Drops AI-Investment Divestiture Proposal in Google Search Case
corrected_draft.description_short: DOJ dropped its proposal to require Google to sell AI investments, while continuing to seek a Chrome sale and other remedies in the search-monopoly case.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department dropped its proposal to require Google to sell its investments in AI companies, including Anthropic. DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued to seek a Chrome divestiture and other remedies in the search case. This was a change to proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case; the record’s donor-causality claim is unsupported.
corrected_draft.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice withdrew one element of its proposed remedies in the federal search-monopoly case against Google: it no longer asked the court to require Google to sell its investments in artificial-intelligence companies, including Anthropic. Reuters reported that prosecutors said evidence gathered after an earlier draft proposal indicated that a forced sale could have unintended consequences in the developing AI sector. DOJ and a coalition of 38 state attorneys general continued to seek a court order requiring Google to sell its Chrome browser and to adopt other measures addressing the search monopoly the court had found. Prosecutors also proposed advance notice to the government of future generative-AI investments. The March action therefore changed one remedy proposal; it did not drop or scale back the antitrust case as a whole. The supplied reporting does not establish that campaign or inauguration donations caused this litigation decision.

corrected_draft.title: Kennedy Terminates Former NIAID Director Jeanne Marrazzo in September 2025
corrected_draft.description_short: Marrazzo was demoted from NIAID director in March 2025 and terminated from her NIH job by Kennedy in a Sept. 26 letter, according to contemporaneous reporting.
corrected_draft.description_medium: The Guardian reported that Jeanne Marrazzo was demoted from her position as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in March 2025. It later reported that HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. terminated her NIH appointment in a letter dated September 26. The held entry’s claim of a March firing is inaccurate; the reported termination occurred in September.
corrected_draft.description_long: Jeanne Marrazzo, then director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, was demoted from that leadership position in March 2025, according to an October 2025 report by The Guardian citing the New York Times. The Guardian reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. later terminated her NIH appointment in a letter dated September 26, 2025, without giving an explanation in the letter. The report said Marrazzo had filed a whistleblower complaint weeks earlier alleging retaliation connected to her objections to administration actions affecting vaccine research; that allegation should be attributed to her complaint rather than stated as an established motive. The held entry places the firing in March and groups it with firings of dozens of other scientists, neither of which is established by this source. A corrected entry can document the September termination and identify the earlier demotion as a separate personnel action.

corrected_draft.title: DHS Revokes Harvard’s Student Exchange Certification
corrected_draft.description_short: DHS revoked Harvard’s SEVP certification on May 22, 2025; a judge blocked the action the next day. This concerned university certification, not individual visa revocations.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On May 22, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem notified Harvard that DHS had revoked its Student and Exchange Visitor Program certification, effective immediately. Harvard filed suit the next day, and a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking the action. The university-level certification dispute threatened its ability to host F- and J-visa students; it does not establish that dozens of individual student visas were revoked.
corrected_draft.description_long: On May 22, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem sent Harvard a letter revoking the university’s Student and Exchange Visitor Program certification, effective immediately. The letter cited Harvard’s response to an April 16 request for records concerning international students. Harvard filed suit and sought a temporary restraining order on May 23; a federal judge granted the request that day, blocking the administration from implementing the revocation while the case proceeded. Harvard’s international students made up about one-quarter of its student body, and the administration’s action threatened the university’s ability to host students and scholars in F- and J-visa categories. This was a university-level certification action. It should not be described as the revocation of dozens of individual students’ visas in May. Later presidential visa restrictions were separate actions and should be recorded separately if relevant. A later court filing records DHS’s May 28 notice of intent to withdraw the certification and a June 20 preliminary injunction against the May letter; the government later stipulated that it would not rely on the letter to revoke Harvard’s certification.
